v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. (2021) 9 SCC 657).
13. Learned Counsel for the Review Petitioner submitted that this
Tribunal has in the judgement under review held that the “Effective
Date” would be the date of signing of the supplementary PPA i.e. 26th
November, 2016. Regulation 8.5 of the PPA dated 28th June, 2016
provides 12 months to Commission the plants from the effective date.
It is argued that the date by which the plant was to be commissioned
by the 1st Respondent was 26th November, 2017 but the plant has
been admittedly commissioned on 8th January, 2018 with a delay of
43 days. It is argued that despite the same, this Tribunal has
observed in paragraph No. 49 of the judgement under review that the
1st Respondent has achieved commercial operation of the solar
power project within the stipulated period of 12 months from the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 14 of 23

“Effective Date” which constitutes the error on the face of record and
as a consequence of such delay in commissioning of the project, the
Respondent No. 1 is liable to pay liquidated damages and reduction
in tariff to Rs.4.36 per unit during the duration of the PPA.
14. We do find force in the submissions of the Learned Senior
Counsel for the Review Petitioner that the solar power plant having
been commissioned on 8th January, 2018 cannot be said to have
been commissioned within the 12 months from the “Effective Date”.
However, despite the same, such findings would not have any
bearing upon the final outcome of the appeals for the reason that we
have concluded in paragraph No. 57 of the judgement under review
that delay beyond SCOD was attributable to statutory authorities and
not to the power developer i.e. the 1st Respondent. We have held that
the 1st Respondent was prevented from fulfilling the conditions
precedented as well as in achieving SCOD of the project by the
delayed actions of Government instrumentality i.e. KREDL & KPTCL
which certainly constitute Force Majeure events in terms of clause
14.3 of the PPA. It would be pertinent to note here that these findings
in the judgement under review have been affirmed by the Hon’ble
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 15 of 23

Supreme Court by dismissing the civil appeals preferred by the
Review Petitioner as noted hereinabove.
15. Therefore, no case has been made out for re-visit of the
judgement under review on this ground.
16. Next, it is argued by the Learned Counsel for the Review
Petitioner that this Tribunal has erred in holding that KPTCL delayed
grant of evacuation approval. It is argued that this Tribunal has failed
to appreciate the fact that after a timely grant of first regular
evacuation approval of 3rd December, 2016, Adani – 1st Respondent
made a fresh application seeking evacuation of power from an
alternate location on 13th March, 2017 i.e. just after of three months
for which KPTCL granted timely approvals on 21st June, 2017. It is
further submitted that thus the Respondent No. 1 had to achieve the
conditions precedent by 26.07.2017 and there was no delay on the
part of KPTCL in granting the evacuation approval. It is argued that
this aspect has been overlooked by this Tribunal.
17. Further submission of the Learned Counsel for the Review
Petitioner is that even if it is assumed for the sake of arguments that
KPTCL had delayed granting the evacuation approval, then also the
default is on the part of the KPTCL which is not even a party to the
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 16 of 23

PPA and therefore, the Review Petitioner cannot be penalized for any
such default on the part of KPTCL. It is submitted that the appropriate
relief available to Respondent No. 1 in these circumstances was
under Article 1.7 and not Article 1.4 of the PPA. On this aspect
reliance is placed on the decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in
Chamundeshwari Electricity Supply Company Ltd. v. Saisudhir
Energy (Chitradurga) Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1816.
18. In this regard, it is to be noted that these very submissions have
been considered and discussed by this Tribunal in paragraph Nos. 55
& 56 of the judgement. We have observed that even if it is accepted
that KPTCL had granted tentative evacuation scheme as well as
regular evacuation scheme approvals in reasonable time still it was
difficult for the developers i.e 1st Respondent to proceed further with
the project before receipt of final approval of the evacuation scheme
which happened only in December, 2016. Even if we accept the
contention raised by the Review Petitioner that the final revised
evacuation approval was granted in this case by KPTCL on 21st June,
2017, it is evident that KPTCL took more than three months in
granting the same. This would be another instance of delay on the
part of KPTCL in granting evacuation approval.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 17 of 23

19. In para 61 of the judgement under review, we have referred to
the letter dated 28th July, 2017 addressed in this regard by the
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Government of India to the
State Governments stating that competent authority only can allow
extension of time as per contractual agreements on account of delay
in connectivity approvals as well as land conversion. In paragraph No.
62 of the judgement under review, while relying upon the earlier
judgement of this Tribunal in Chennamangathihalli Solar Power
Project LLP and Ors. Vs. BESCOM and Ors. 2020 SCC Online
APTEL 75, this Tribunal has observed that delay in grant of approvals
by the Government instrumentalities constitutes Force Majeure event
entitling the developers for extension of SCOD.
20. Notably, these findings have been affirmed by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court while dismissing the civil appeals filed by the Review
Petitioner.
21. Hence, we do not find any error in the judgement under review
on this ground also as agitated on behalf of the review petitioner.
22. Next ground on which review of the judgement dated 14th May,
2024 is sought by the Review Petitioner is that this Tribunal has erred
in holding that KREDL delayed grant of land conversion in favour of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 18 of 23

Respondent No. 1. Learned Counsel for Review Petitioner submitted
that Respondent No. 1 applied to KREDL on 26th May, 2017 for land
conversion i.e. just two months prior to achieving conditions
precedent with incomplete documents which was highlighted for
KREDL vide letters dated 7th June, 2017 and 23rd March, 2019, but
Respondent No. 1 did not respond to the same. It is further submitted
that after lapse of 14 months from the date of achieving the conditions
precedent, Respondent No. 1 abandoned its previous application for
land conversion and made a fresh proposal to Deputy Commissioner,
Ramanagara on 24th September, 2018 which shows that Respondent
No. 1 failed to hold title of the land within the stipulated time. It is
argued that these facts indicate that Respondent No. 1 alone is at
fault for having applied for land conversion belatedly and that too
without requisite document. It is argued that evidently Respondent
No. 1 failed to pursue the land acquisition and conversion in a timely
manner for which KREDL cannot be held responsible and therefore,
the findings on this aspect in the judgment under review suffers from
a patent error which needs to be rectified.
23. In this regard, we note that in view of the circular dated 22nd
February, 2016 issued by the Government of Karnataka, KREDL was
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 19 of 23

to obtain agricultural land from the agriculturists and to make the
same available to the developers for sub-lease. We have noted this
fact in paragraph No. 59 of the judgement under review and have
observed that on account of delay on the part of the KREDL in
completing the said process to make agricultural land available to the
1st Respondent on sub-lease, the 1st Respondent was constrained to
approach KREDL on 25th May, 2017 for such approval/sub-lease. In
paragraph No. 60, we have noted that nothing has been brought to
our notice from the record to show that KREDL had obtained the
agricultural land from the land owners on lease basis more than 60
days before the date on which conditions precedent had to be
achieved by 1st Respondent. We have noted that before holding the
1st Respondent responsible, it was necessary for KREDL and KPTCL
to specify the dates on which the land had been obtained on lease
from the agriculturists and the 1st Respondent was asked to take on
sub-lease. In the absence of any such evidence of record, we did not
find it appropriate to hold the 1st Respondent responsible for delay in
taking necessary approvals from the concerned authorities for taking
the land required for the power project on sub-lease and obtaining
conversion of the land use from agricultural to non-agricultural. Even
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 20 of 23

nothing in this regard has been pointed out from the record by the
Learned Counsel for the Review Petitioner during the course of
arguments on this Review Petition also.
24. Therefore, the argument that the judgement under review
suffers from any error apparent on the face of record on this aspect
is absolutely baseless and devoid of any merit.
25. Lastly, it is contended on behalf of the Review Petitioner that in
paragraph 57 of the judgement under review, this Tribunal has
extracted paragraph No. 17(d) of the order passed by the
Commission but the said extracted paragraph of the Commission’s
order cannot be found in the order dated 10th July, 2020 passed by
the Commission in O.P. No. 17 of 2020 which had been filed by the
Review Petitioner and, therefore, such patent error ought to be
rectified.
26. On this aspect, we note that what we have reproduced in
paragraph No. 57 of the judgement under review is paragraph No.
17(d) of the order dated 27th July, 2020 passed by the Commission in
the petition filed by the 1st Respondent which was under challenge in
Appeal No. 181 of 2020 (one of appeals in these batch of appeals
which were decided by way of the judgement under review dated 14th
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 21 of 23

May, 2024) which had been taken as a lead appeal in the batch.
Therefore, it is not correct to say that this paragraph No. 17(d) does
not appear in any of the orders passed by the Commission which had
been challenged in this batch of appeals.
27. Thus, it is evident that there is elaborate discussion in the
judgement under review on each of the issues which have been
agitated by the Review Petitioner in this petition. In the judgement
under review, this Tribunal has come to a particular finding upon
consideration of the relevant contractual provisions as well as the rival
submissions of the Learned Counsel for the parties which has been
affirmed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and therefore, those findings
cannot be altered in the review proceedings. Well reasoned and well
considered judgement, even though erroneous, does not fall within
the ambit of review. There is a clear distinction between a judgement
suffering from error patent on the face of record and erroneous
judgement. Review Petition is maintainable only on the former case
whereas in the latter case the remedy available to the aggrieved party
is to assail the order/judgement by way of appeal in the higher
forum/Court.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 13 of 2025 Page 22 of 23

28. By way of the instant review petition, the petitioner is actually
seeking a relook of the judgment under review in the hope to
discover any flaw or fault in the same, which is not permissible in
law. The review petition manifestly appears to be appeal in disguise
and thus, does not fall within the scope and ambit of Order XLVII
Rule 1 of the CPC.
29. Hence, we are of the considered opinion that the petitioner has
failed to make out any mistake or error apparent on the face of
record in the judgment under review dated 14.05.2024 and has
failed to bring the case within the parameters laid down by the
Hon'ble Supreme Court in various decisions referred to
hereinabove. The review petition is sans any merit and is
accordingly dismissed.
Pronounced in the open court on this 15th day of July, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

ORDER
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. In this application, the Appellant has made following prayers :-
“(a) Direct Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to pay Rs.
1,70,58,404, as an interim measure, towards the
outstanding as per the interim tariff of Rs. 2.43 per unit for
the period October 2017 to July 2018, and for March & May
2020 or set aside the impugned order dated 07.07.2021
passed by Ld. APERC in OP No. 60 of 2019;
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 2 of 10

(b) Direct Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to pay 50% of the
total outstanding as per the tariff of Rs. 4.84 per unit to
GIWSL till December 2020;
(c) Direct Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to set up a Letter of
Credit in favour of GIWSL under Article 5.4 of the PPA; and
(d) Pass such other orders as this Hon'ble Tribunal
deems fit.
2. We have heard Learned Counsel for the Appellant and have
perused the written note of arguments submitted on behalf of
Respondent No. 2.
3. It appears that the Appellant had filed petition bearing O.P. NO.
60 of 2019 before the Commission seeking recovery of pending
monthly bills from Respondent No. 2 for supply of power in terms of
Power Purchase Agreement dated 18th February, 2017 along with
carrying cost and late payment surcharge. The Appellant had also
sought direction against Respondent No. 2 for setting up a payment
security management by way of opening a letter of credit in favour of
Appellant as mandated under the PPA and not to deduct any amount
as Generation Based Incentive from the tariff payable to Appellant.
The prayers made in the petition are extracted hereinbelow:-
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 3 of 10

“(a) To direct APSPDCL/APPCC to release payments due
to GIWSL set out in paragraph 3 of the petition which have
been unlawfully withheld;
(b) to direct APSPDCL to set up a payment security
mechanism as required under the PPA;
(c) to direct APSPDCL/APPCC to pay 75% of the
outstanding amounts to GIWSL within one week, pending
final adjudication.
(d) to direct the respondents to pay carrying cost to the
petitioner to be determined by the Commission.”
4. The petition was disposed off by the Commission vide order
dated 7th July, 2021 which has been impugned in this appeal. The
relevant portion of the impugned order is reproduced hereinbelow:-
“We have heard Sri Rohit Venkat, learned Counsel for the
petitioner and Sri P. Shiva Rao, learned Counsel for the
respondents.
As regards prayers (a) and (c) which are substantive in
nature, they have become infructuous in view of the
payment made at the interim tariff fixed by the Hon'ble High
Court in W.P.No.9844 of 2019.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 4 of 10

It is not in dispute that the issue of review of the PPAs
which is the subject matter of O.P.No.17 of 2019 is sub
judice before a Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court in
a batch of Writ Appeals. In the said cases, interim order of
stay of adjudication of O.P.No.17 of 2019 has been
granted and the same is in force. In the light of these facts,
it is not possible for the Commission to adjudicate the
issues raised by the petitioner at this stage as regards the
PPA tariff. The prayers (b) and (d) being ancillary to the
main prayers, the Commission is of the opinion that the
same may be adjudicated at an appropriate time.
Accordingly, the O.P. is disposed of without prejudice to
the right of the petitioner to agitate the prayers made in (b)
and (d) after disposal of the batch of Writ Appeals pending
before the Hon'ble High Court.”
5. The Appellant has assailed the said order of the Commission
on following grounds interalia :-
“(a) Ld. APERC has erroneously held that GIWSL's
prayer seeking directions to APSPDCL to release
payments in accordance with the PPA has been rendered
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 5 of 10

infructuous in view of the payment made at the interim tariff
of Rs. 2.43 per unit, without appreciating that GIWSL's
claim before Ld. APERC was for APSPDCL to make
payment of full tariff as specified under Article 2.2 of the
PPA i.e., @ Rs. 4.84 per unit.
(b) Without prejudice to the above, Ld. APERC failed to
appreciate that APSPDCL has not made payments to
GIWSL for all months even at the interim tariff of Rs. 2.43
per unit. It is pertinent to note that even at the interim tariff,
Rs. 1,59,18,108 for the period October 2017 to July 2018
and Rs. 11,40,296 for the months of March 2020 and May
2020 is due and pending.
(c) Ld. APERC's finding of payment having been made
to GIWSL as per Order dated 24.09.2019 in W.P. No. 9844
of 2019 and batch is contrary to the record. In fact, there is
nothing on record to prove that the payments have been
made. Thus, Ld. APERC failed to make a proper inquiry
into the facts of the matter and arrived at the conclusion
qua payment of dues by APSPDCL without any
reasonable basis.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 6 of 10

(d) Ld. APERC has wrongly concluded that the prayer
for opening payment security mechanism/LC is ancillary to
the main prayer. The obligation of APSPDCL to set up LC
in favour of GIWSL under the PPA is independent of
payment to be made towards monthly bills by APSPDCL
to GIWSL under the PPA. APSPDCL's obligation to set up
payment security mechanism/LC is mandated not only
under Article 5.4 of the PPA, but also under Clause 6.2 of
the National Tariff Policy 2016 and the Ministry of Power
("MoP") Notifications dated 28.06.2019, 23.07.2019 and
31.07.2019.
(e) Ld. APERC failed to return any finding on claims
raised by GIWSL in its petition towards wrongful deduction
of GBI component by APSPDCL from tariff payable to
GIWSL and liability of APSPDCL to pay LPS on delayed
/pending bills. The amount towards GBI is being withheld
contrary to the order dated 05.10.2018 passed by this
Hon'ble Tribunal in Appeal No. 284 of 2018.
(f) By failing to adjudicate the issues raised by GIWSL
in the petition, Ld. APERC has failed to discharge its
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 7 of 10

statutory functions under Sections 86(1)(f) and 86(1)(e) of
the Electricity Act, 2003.”
6. The prayers made in this appeal by the Appellant are as under:-
“(a) Set aside the Impugned Order dated 07.07.2021
passed by Ld. APERC in O.P. No. 60 of 2019;
(b) Direct Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to pay Rs.
59,92,96,545 (at PPA tariff of Rs. 4.84/unit) towards
monthly bills raised by GIWSL till December 2020, along
with Late Payment Surcharge/Carrying Cost as per Article
5.2 of the PPA;
(c) Direct Respondent Nos 2 and 3 to pay future monthly
bills on or before their respective due dates under the PPA,
(d) Direct Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 to set up a Letter of
Credit in favour of GIWSL under Article 5.4 of the PPA;
(e) Award interest at the rate of 8.32% in favour of GIWSL,
and
(f) Pass any such other and further reliefs as this Hon'ble
Tribunal deems just and proper in the nature and
circumstances of the present case.”
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 8 of 10

7. During the course of hearing of application under disposal, the
thrust of the Learned Counsel for the Appellant was only with regards
to the prayer (c) i.e. direction to Respondent Nos. 2 & 3 to set up a
letter of credit in favour of Appellant under Regulation 5.4 of the PPA.
8. We note that this prayer in the interim application is identical to
the prayer (d) made in the appeal, which has been extracted
hereinabove. Therefore, we concur with the contentions agitated on
behalf of Respondent No. 2 that granting of such interim relief in this
application would tantamount to granting the final relief as made in
the appeal.
9. Be that as it may, we feel concerned about the perfunctory
manner in which the Commission has dealt with the Appellant’s
petition in the impugned order. A bare look at the impugned order
would reveal that the same is cryptic and sans any reasons and has
been passed without discussing the rival contentions of the parties.
Therefore, we find it appropriate to, instead of passing any directions
in the interim application under disposal, to take up the appeal itself
for final disposal.
10. The parties shall explain on the next date as to why the case
may not be remanded back to the Commission for reconsideration
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IA No. 1488 of 2021 Page 9 of 10

and for passing a fresh reasoned order upon taking note of the rival
contentions/submissions of the parties.
11. List on 05.08.2026.
Pronounced in the open court on this 15th day of July, 2026.
(Virender Bhat) (Seema Gupta)
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson
